items.title: Math Can’t Go On Like This
items.author: Kai Williams
items.blurb: Kai Williams reports from the International Congress of Mathematicians, where Terence Tao warned of a ‘crisis in our mathematical values and practices’ weeks before OpenAI announced its bots had cracked Navier–Stokes.

items.title: Why the NIH must resist the metrics trap
items.author: Kirsten K. Davison
items.blurb: The NIH, the world’s largest funder of health research, is consulting on how to measure and incentivize research impact; Davison warns this rare, time-sensitive chance to get evaluation right may be squandered.

items.title: Which million-dollar math problem could AI solve next?
items.author: Manon Bischoff
items.blurb: A week after an OpenAI model presented a possible Navier–Stokes solution, mathematicians are speculating about which of the remaining Millennium Prize problems could fall next.

items.title: Making AI safer is not impossible, but agreeing to do so may be
items.blurb: American AI labs and the American authorities are at odds over slowing frontier research, and so are America and China — making the technical problem of safety the easier half.

items.title: Make AI traceable before it shapes global climate assessments
items.author: Carlos Garcia-Soto
items.blurb: With the IPCC building AI support for literature reviews and reviewer comments, Garcia-Soto argues that AI tools can change a report’s findings before a single word is written, so their use must be traceable upstream.

items.title: AI tool turns any paper into an ‘agent’ that can collaborate and answer complex queries
items.author: Kaia Glickman
items.blurb: A Stanford framework called Paper2Agent converts a paper and its code into a ‘virtual corresponding author’ that answers questions, reruns the analyses on new data and collaborates with other paper-agents; the authors pitch it as a new test of whether a paper is reproducible at all.

items.title: AI companies must work with the research community to protect attribution
items.blurb: Nature’s editorial on the 8 September Millennium Prize claim: an epoch-making result raises a hard question about how AI tools credit the earlier human work they build on, and the labs must work out attribution with researchers rather than around them.

items.title: Anthropic’s AI steals mathematicians’ record for most complicated curve
items.author: Manon Bischoff
items.blurb: It took mathematicians more than 18 years to go from rank-28 to rank-29 elliptic curves; Manon Bischoff reports that Claude found a curve of rank at least 31 in days, taking the number-theory record.

items.title: AI co-scientists are revolutionizing how research is done
items.author: Elie Dolgin
items.blurb: Elie Dolgin surveys the AI ‘co-scientist’ systems now generating hypotheses, designing experiments and analysing data in labs — and finds that humans are still the ones who have to decide what makes sense.

items.title: Did OpenAI solve the wrong Navier-Stokes problem?
items.blurb: OpenAI’s Navier–Stokes proof appears eligible for the $1-million Millennium Prize — but, Scientific American reports, only by way of a controversial loophole in how the problem is posed.

items.title: What’s Really Behind the Baby Bust?
items.author: Margaret Talbot
items.blurb: Reviewing Anna Louise Sussman’s ‘Inconceivable’, Margaret Talbot asks why people say they want more children than they have — whether modern life is stopping them, or our ideas about a good life have changed.

items.title: China punishes prominent academics exposed by research sleuth
items.author: Xiaoying You
items.blurb: Several prominent Chinese scientists investigated for research-integrity violations by the video-blogger ‘Student Geng’ have now faced disciplinary measures, Xiaoying You reports — a rare case of a public sleuth forcing institutional action.

items.title: What a Trump order to put political appointees in charge of NIH funding would mean for science
items.blurb: Advocates and scientists warn that a reported executive order giving political appointees power over NIH research grants would ‘upend’ U.S. science and its peer-review system.

items.title: Members of Congress push back on plan to create a commission of political appointees to review NIH grants
items.author: Anil Oza and Chelsea Cirruzzo
items.blurb: OMB director Russell Vought is pushing an executive order that would create a commission — including himself and NIH director Jay Bhattacharya, with unanimous sign-off required — to review every NIH grant; several members of Congress have voiced strong opposition.

items.title: Further results on AI and labor market reallocation
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: Cowen flags a new paper that combines CPS and JOLTS data with OpenAI and Lightcast measures of AI exposure and adoption to document how AI has changed stocks and flows in the US labour market.

items.title: How we can beat China
items.author: Noah Smith
items.blurb: Noah Smith argues that the way for America to beat China is to let China beat itself.

items.title: China Still Has What America Needs
items.author: Adam S. Posen
items.blurb: Adam Posen argues that China still holds what the American economy needs, and that the Trump–Xi summit gives Washington a chance to buy time.

items.title: UK productivity higher than we had thought
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: New official figures show UK productivity rose at almost twice the pace previously estimated in the decade after the 2008 financial crisis, making Britain look much less of an international outlier.

items.title: Mathematicians use AI to find mysterious symmetries, solving decades-old problem
items.blurb: Six mathematicians used AI to spot symmetries and approximate polynomials, finding a degree-23 polynomial that settles the inverse Galois problem for the sporadic group M₂₃ — while a parallel crowdsourced race found all 25,000 cases for 24 roots, with humans using minimal AI winning.

items.title: Why mathematicians are hiding research results in zero-knowledge proofs
items.blurb: Google used a zero-knowledge proof to show quantum computers could break encryption by decade’s end without revealing the algorithm; outside experts reproduced and improved the result within weeks, a test case for whether secrecy can survive in mathematics.

items.title: Hundreds of ‘free’ academic journals have started charging fees
items.author: Dalmeet Singh Chawla
items.blurb: A study tracking diamond open-access journals finds a growing number of ‘free’ titles switching to fee-charging models — especially over the past few years — Dalmeet Singh Chawla reports.

items.title: Will AI really kill us all? The science behind the hype
items.author: Elizabeth Gibney
items.blurb: Elizabeth Gibney examines the science behind claims that AI might spell the end for humanity, and why AI companies themselves are now calling for a slowdown.

items.title: The economics of late grandmotherhood
items.author: Tyler Cowen
items.blurb: A new paper shows how fertility delays compound across generations: under the 1960 first-birth schedule median grandmotherhood came at 44; under the 2024 schedule it is 57, cutting into the healthy years grandmothers have with grandchildren.

items.title: In MAGA-land people are dying faster than they are being born
items.blurb: The Economist’s analysis finds deaths now outnumber births across Trump country, so it is growing only because of migration.
